propositions.text: Whether former union members have standing to maintain judicial review of an adjudicator's negative decision when no longer represented by their union but authorized by it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether former union members have standing for judicial review without union representation but with union authorization.

propositions.text: The issue arises in the following factual context.

paragraphs.summary: The court introduces the factual context for the issue.

propositions.text: Applicants were employed by Canada Revenue Agency as large-file appeals officers at AU-04 level in Calgary and were members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada with a collective agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants' employment and union membership facts.

propositions.text: Applicants filed grievances alleging employer violated clause 45.07 requiring acting pay for duties of higher classification for three consecutive days.
Applicants alleged they performed duties of AU-05 and AU-06 positions for a lengthy period.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants filed grievances alleging acting pay violations and performing higher classification duties.

propositions.text: Grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication under subsection 209(1) of FPSLR Act.
Applicants obtained Institute's approval to represent them in adjudication as required by subsection 209(2).

paragraphs.summary: The court states grievances were consolidated and applicants obtained union approval for adjudication representation.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found no jurisdiction as issues were classification, not acting pay.
If jurisdiction existed, Institute failed to show grievors assigned work outside AU-04 job description.

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator found no jurisdiction and that the Institute failed to prove work outside job description.

propositions.text: Institute retained counsel for judicial review and filed applications for each applicant.
Applicants decided to represent themselves after discussions with Institute and have done so since.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Institute retained counsel but applicants chose self-representation for judicial review.

propositions.text: Respondent Attorney General argues applicants lack standing to pursue application.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues applicants lack standing to pursue the application.

propositions.text: Institute granted intervenor status on standing issue.
Institute's General Counsel swore affidavit authorizing and supporting continuation of application.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute was intervenor and its counsel swore affidavit supporting continuation of application.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review consolidated with others after procedural removals of parties.
Reasons to be placed in each file.

paragraphs.summary: The court consolidated applications and ordered reasons placed in each file.

propositions.text: Issues: standing to pursue judicial review, adjudicator's jurisdiction error, procedural fairness breach, reasonable apprehension of bias, reliance on perjured evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames issues including standing, jurisdiction, fairness, bias, and perjured evidence.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants not directly affected persons under subsection 18.1(1) Federal Courts Act.
Applicants seek benefit under collective agreement but are not parties to contract exclusively between Institute and Canada Revenue Agency.
Exclusivity principle means only union can pursue grievance.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues applicants lack standing as they are not parties to the collective agreement and only the union can pursue grievances.

propositions.text: Applicant Ken Insch argues he has statutory and common law standing under FPSLR Act subsection 209(2).
He signed the grievance and Institute supports the application.
He is directly affected by adjudicator's denial of acting pay and alleged fraud, perjury, and egregious conduct.
Government owed him a duty of fairness; other applicants adopt these submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues he has standing, signed grievance, is directly affected, and alleges unfair conduct; others adopt this.

propositions.text: Institute acknowledges it must support judicial review applications relating to collective agreement interpretation or administration.
Citing cases, Institute submits only union has carriage of disputes before Board on collective agreement interpretation and application.
This ensures individual members cannot advance unsupported arguments about collective agreement interpretation or application.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits only the union can carry disputes on collective agreement interpretation to ensure unified representation.

propositions.text: Institute submits grievance and adjudication scheme under FPSLR Act differs as individual grievor files grievance in their name.
Under this scheme, grievor becomes applicant or respondent in judicial review of adjudicator's decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits the FPSLR Act scheme allows individual grievor to file grievance and be applicant in judicial review.

propositions.text: Institute submits it must continue to support judicial review applications to maintain autonomy policing collective agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute argues it must support judicial review applications to maintain its autonomy in policing the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Before considering issue, court refers to relevant collective agreement and FPSLR Act provisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court refers to relevant collective agreement and FPSLR Act provisions before considering the issue.

propositions.text: Collective agreement is between Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the collective agreement is between the Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

propositions.text: Article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees covered by certificate issued December 12, 2001.
Applicants were employees described in this certificate.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees including applicants.

propositions.text: No provision grants individual employee unfettered right to pursue grievance if grievance relates to collective agreement interpretation or application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no provision grants individual employees unfettered right to pursue grievances on collective agreement interpretation.

propositions.text: Article 34 of the agreement deals with the grievance procedure.
Article 34.07 prevents an employee from presenting an individual grievance without Institute approval and representation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 34 governs grievance procedure and article 34.07 requires Institute approval for individual grievances.

propositions.text: Article 34.22 precludes an employee from referring an individual grievance to adjudication without Institute approval.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 34.22 requires Institute approval before referring individual grievances to adjudication.

propositions.text: Article 34 provisions largely reflect legislated requirements in the FPSLR Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes article 34 largely reflects legislated requirements in the FPSLR Act.

propositions.text: The FPSLR Act preamble recognizes mutual respect and harmonious labour-management relations as essential.
The preamble recognizes bargaining agents represent employees' interests in collective bargaining and dispute resolution.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the FPSLR Act preamble recognizes mutual respect and bargaining agents' role in employee representation.

propositions.text: Subsection 2(1) defines collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent on employment terms.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 2(1) defines collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent.

propositions.text: Part 1 defines parties as employer and bargaining agent in collective bargaining contexts.
Part 2 of the Act, dealing with grievances, contains no definition of parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Part 1 defines parties as employer and bargaining agent; Part 2 has no parties definition.

propositions.text: Subsection 208(1) entitles an employee to present an individual grievance if aggrieved by collective agreement interpretation or application.
Subsection 208(4) requires employee to have bargaining agent approval and representation to present grievance.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 208(1) allows individual grievances with bargaining agent approval per 208(4).

propositions.text: Subsection 209(1) permits referral of individual grievance to adjudication relating to collective agreement interpretation or application.
Subsection 209(2) requires bargaining agent approval before referring grievance to adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 209(1) permits grievance referral to adjudication with bargaining agent approval per 209(2).

propositions.text: Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Regulations reflect these provisions.
Section 67 permits employee to present individual grievance.
Subsection 69(1) requires declaration from bargaining agent approving and representing grievor.
Subsection 89(1) requires notice of reference to adjudication in Form 20 with bargaining agent declaration per 89(3).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Regulations require bargaining agent approval and declarations for individual grievances and adjudication notices.

propositions.text: Adjudication rights arise from legislation, not the collective agreement.
Subsections 208(1) and 209(1) entitle employees like applicants to present grievances and refer them to adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adjudication rights arise from legislation, entitling applicants to present grievances and refer them to adjudication.

propositions.text: Parties to adjudication are individual grievors and employer; union approves and represents but is not a party.
Applicants are not exercising adjudication rights under the collective agreement between Institute and Canada Revenue Agency.
Attorney General submits applicants exercise adjudication rights under the collective agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties to adjudication are grievors and employer; union is not a party; Attorney General's contrary submission is rejected.

propositions.text: Legislative scheme ousts contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the legislative scheme ousts the contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General.

propositions.text: Subsection 18.1(1) of Federal Courts Act permits anyone directly affected to apply for judicial review.
Attorney General argues applicants are not directly affected and lack standing.
Attorney General has not demonstrated applicants lack standing; applicants have standing to pursue judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Federal Courts Act allows judicial review by those directly affected; Attorney General's standing argument fails; applicants have standing.

propositions.text: Acknowledges difficulty posed by legislative scheme to union's role at judicial review stage.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges the legislative scheme poses difficulty for union's role at judicial review stage.

propositions.text: Board and predecessors hold grievance requires bargaining agent representation to proceed.
If bargaining agent withdraws support, grievance is no longer adjudicable.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Board's consistent finding that grievances require bargaining agent representation and lose adjudicability if support withdrawn.

propositions.text: No similar statutory requirement exists for judicial review of adjudicator's negative decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no statutory requirement for union representation at judicial review of adjudicator's decision.

propositions.text: Judicial review involves rights of all union members; union representation protects bargaining unit interests at grievance and adjudication stages.
It makes little sense to lose union representation protection at judicial review, which has greater precedential value.
Legislation provides no solution when union member pursues judicial review but union does not.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds union representation protects members' rights at grievance and adjudication; losing it at judicial review is problematic; legislation lacks solution.

propositions.text: Institute submits union maintains ultimate control of grievance as it will represent grievors if matter remitted.
Court rejects this, noting potential for binding directions or outcome from this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Institute's submission that union controls grievance on judicial review, noting court's power to issue binding directions.

propositions.text: Institute counsel drafted notice of application for judicial review.
Applicants argue inadequate representation by Institute and allege employer presented perjured evidence.
Such serious unfiltered perjury allegation against co-workers may harm harmonious labour-management relations.
Absence of union representation on judicial review may lead to such consequences.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Institute drafted application; applicants allege inadequate representation and perjury; absence of union may harm labour relations.

propositions.text: Is there a way to recognize union's responsibility to protect bargaining unit interests on judicial review?

paragraphs.summary: The court raises issue of how to respect union's responsibility to protect bargaining unit interests on judicial review.

propositions.text: Rule 303(1) requires applicants to name as respondents every person directly affected by the order sought, except the tribunal.
Applicants no longer represented by their union may be required to name the union as respondent and serve notice on it.
Compliance with Rule 303(1) ensures affected unions receive notice and can participate to protect bargaining unit interests.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 303(1) requires naming affected respondents, possibly including unions, to ensure their participation and protection of bargaining unit interests.

propositions.text: Whether the adjudicator committed a reviewable error in finding she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the grievances.

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether the adjudicator erred in finding lack of jurisdiction over the grievances.

propositions.text: The standard of review of correctness should apply to the adjudicator's finding of lack of jurisdiction.
The adjudicator's decision on jurisdiction is reviewed for reasonableness, not correctness, citing Nadeau and Klos cases.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue correctness standard applies to jurisdiction finding; court finds reasonableness standard applies, citing precedents.

propositions.text: The adjudicator erred in law by misconstruing grievances as classification issues, constituting abuse of discretion and jurisdiction error.
There is no merit to the applicants' submission of error of law or abuse of discretion by the adjudicator.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances; court finds no merit in this submission.

propositions.text: Applicants made few submissions addressing adjudicator's jurisdiction finding and do not point to clear errors in reasoning.
Applicants focus on arguing their case de novo and on fraudulent concealment, which the Board did not determine due to lack of jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicants did not challenge adjudicator's jurisdiction reasoning but focused on new arguments and fraudulent concealment.

propositions.text: Adjudicator referred to Bungay decision describing characteristics distinguishing classification from acting pay grievances.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the adjudicator referred to Bungay decision describing grievance distinctions.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns related to all duties since appointment and consistent over time, suggesting chronic undervaluation.

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns about consistent duties suggested chronic undervaluation.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found applicants' grievances related to classification based on evidence appreciation, a determination entitled to deference.
Applicants have not shown the adjudicator's classification finding was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found grievances related to classification; court defers and finds no unreasonableness shown by applicants.

propositions.text: Adjudicator breached procedural fairness by excluding some applicant evidence but allowing employer evidence, causing bias.
Adjudicator showed reasonable apprehension of bias by relying almost exclusively on employer testimony despite equal applicant credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege procedural fairness breach and bias due to exclusion of their evidence and reliance on employer testimony.

propositions.text: Evidence was excluded as from outside the grievance period.
No transcript exists; court relies on affidavit evidence to assess exclusion reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say evidence was excluded for being outside grievance period; court notes reliance on affidavits due to no transcript.

propositions.text: Adjudicator excluded June 2, 2005 memorandum because sender/contact did not testify and it related to Audit Division, not Appeals Division.
Exclusion of memorandum justified; employer's representative evidence unchallenged in cross-examination.

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator excluded a memorandum due to lack of testimony and relevance; exclusion justified and unchallenged.

propositions.text: March 21, 2003 memorandum excluded because bargaining agent could not connect it to applicant witness; no testimony from sender/recipient.
Exclusion of this memorandum also justified.

paragraphs.summary: Another memorandum was excluded due to lack of connection to witness and testimony; exclusion justified.

propositions.text: Similar examples of evidence exclusion exist.

paragraphs.summary: There are other similar examples of evidence exclusion by the adjudicator.

propositions.text: Courts should not substitute their view of evidence relevance for decision-maker's except when exclusion breaches natural justice.
Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières v. Larocque states exclusion of relevant evidence must impact fairness to breach natural justice.
Adjudicator dismissed evidence for reasons beyond grievance period, not solely on that basis.

paragraphs.summary: Court states it defers to decision-maker on evidence exclusion unless natural justice breached; adjudicator excluded evidence for multiple reasons.

propositions.text: No basis to find documents were improperly excluded causing breach of natural justice or bias without better evidence from applicants.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no basis to conclude improper exclusion of documents breached natural justice or caused bias without better evidence.

propositions.text: Adjudicator's reliance on employer evidence does not support bias allegation; bias is serious and requires strong evidence.
Committee for Justice and Liberty v. Canada requires reasonable apprehension of bias to be likely to affect fairness.
Applicants have not shown reasonable, informed person would likely think adjudicator unfair; disagreement with evidence assessment is insufficient.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no bias as applicants failed to show reasonable apprehension; mere disagreement with evidence assessment is insufficient.

propositions.text: Canada Revenue Agency employees submitted perjured evidence.
Perjury is serious and must be supported by more than mere assertion, citing Rafizadeh v. Toronto-Dominion Bank.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege perjury by CRA employees; court states perjury requires more than mere assertion, citing precedent.

propositions.text: Applicants' allegations of perjury are disagreements with evidence and requests to reweigh evidence before adjudicator.
Applicants have not demonstrated perjury.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicants' perjury claims are mere disagreements and fail to demonstrate perjury.

propositions.text: Dismiss application for judicial review; adjudicator's jurisdiction decision was reasonable and not tainted by bias or impropriety.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application, finding adjudicator's jurisdiction decision reasonable and free of bias or impropriety.

propositions.text: No order as to costs since success on issues was divided.

paragraphs.summary: Court declines to order costs due to divided success on issues.
